motion: Is finite theism preferable to naturalism?

routes.speaker: Philip Goff
routes.position: Finite theism is preferable to naturalism.

bridges.statement: Finite theism is preferable because a simple, purposive but power-limited God jointly explains value-supporting features and suffering better than naturalism.
Fine-tuning is substantially more expected under a good purposive creator than under chance, and does not derive its multiverse support from fine-tuning itself.
Precisely limited divine creative power explains why a good God used a suffering-laden evolutionary process.
Conscious understanding and libertarian purposive agency require more explanation than an appeal to contingent natural selection alone.
Finite monotheism retains substantial simplicity despite qualifying divine power and is simpler than polytheistic or morally mixed alternatives.
Finite theism can remain open about process theism, open theism, divine mentality, and related metaphysical details.

routes.speaker: Graham Oppy
routes.position: Naturalism is preferable to finite theism.

bridges.statement: Naturalism is preferable as the simpler total theory with the better overall fit to the actual evidence.
Goff has not established the modal and probability assumptions needed for fine-tuning to favor finite theism over naturalism.
Worldviews should be compared through simplicity and fit with actual evidence rather than unsupported Bayesian priors or counterfactual evidence.
Identity theory, mental causation, and contingent evolutionary history provide naturalistic resources for consciousness and behavior.
Predictions about what a radically different divine agent would value or create are under-supported.
Nearby finite, process, or anthropocentric theisms expose unresolved choices within Goff's hypothesis.

sections.title: Simplicity, prior probability, and theory comparison
Neighboring theisms, polytheism, and strongest challenges

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: finetuning of physics for life is evidence for some kind of theism
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.proposition: Life requires physical constants in an extremely narrow range, making our life-permitting universe appear highly improbable by chance and evidentially relevant to theism.
moves.inventoryRationale: Introduces the principal fine-tuning datum on which Goff's comparative case depends.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: terrible suffering we find in the world is powerful evidence
Why would a loving God who can do anything
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.proposition: Terrible suffering, especially suffering produced by natural selection, is powerful evidence against an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God.
moves.inventoryRationale: Establishes the negative datum that motivates departing from classical perfect-being theism.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you don't have to choose
fine-tuning in terms of God's purposes
suffering in terms of God's limitations
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.proposition: A good God with limited power can jointly explain fine-tuning through divine purposes and suffering through divine limitations.
moves.inventoryRationale: States Goff's core synthesis and directly supports his side of the motion.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: The only way God can create intelligent life
God can create a universe with that structure, but can't fiddle thereafter
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.proposition: God's precise limitation is the power to select a universe's fundamental structure and constants but not to intervene afterward, leaving evolution as the only route to intelligent life.
moves.inventoryRationale: Specifies the hypothesized power limit that is supposed to explain evolutionary suffering.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the awesome evidence that I've just described will be strong evidence for Islam
the finetuning is strong evidence for theism
moves.attributionBasis: Goff explicitly presents the premises and conclusion of his argument.
moves.proposition: If a Quran inscription in the universe's initial structure would strongly support Islam, then analogous purposive structure in fine-tuning should strongly support theism.
moves.inventoryRationale: Introduces the 'awesome evidence' analogy used throughout the later modal dispute.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: that evidence does not favor a multiverse at all
There's nothing to do with the finetuning
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's uninterrupted probabilistic presentation.
moves.proposition: Once the existence of our universe is backgrounded, its fine-tuning does not favor a multiverse; any nearby multiverse support comes from the universe's mere existence.
moves.inventoryRationale: Distinguishes fine-tuning evidence from evidence that merely fits or supports a multiverse through universe multiplicity.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: natural selection just cares about behavior
sophisticated behavioral functioning without any kind of inner life
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.proposition: Because natural selection selects behavior and sophisticated behavior could occur without inner life, it is unclear why consciousness evolved.
moves.inventoryRationale: States the first form of Goff's psychophysical-harmony challenge to naturalism.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I'm not saying physicalism is false
why non-concious mechanisms couldn't have done the same
meaningless consciousness instead of conceptually rich consciousness
moves.attributionBasis: Goff explicitly qualifies and states his inference.
moves.proposition: Even granting physicalism and the survival value of consciousness, naturalism must explain why nonconscious mechanisms—or meaningless consciousness—did not perform the same functions.
moves.inventoryRationale: Clarifies that the challenge concerns comparative explanation, not a deductive refutation of physicalism.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: another explanation, namely libertarian free will
libertarian free will is a sort of fundamental causal relation
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.proposition: Libertarian freedom supplies a fundamental, rationally responsive causal relation rather than treating psychophysical harmony as directly produced by an all-powerful God.
moves.inventoryRationale: Introduces Goff's proposed intermediary explanation and avoids restoring the problem of evil.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: libertarian free will plus natural selection
natural selection I think has a motivation to give us conscious understanding
moves.attributionBasis: Goff explicitly states his proposed solution.
moves.proposition: Given libertarian rational agency, conscious understanding improves adaptive responses, so natural selection has reason to select it as an efficient survival shortcut.
moves.inventoryRationale: Provides Goff's positive explanation for the evolution of conscious understanding.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: libertarian free will if it exists supports the existence of God
more expected given theism than atheism
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's uninterrupted opening presentation.
moves.proposition: If libertarian freedom is a fundamental potential built into nature from the beginning, its great value makes it more expected under theism than atheism.
moves.inventoryRationale: Turns the freedom hypothesis into independent comparative support for finite theism.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: typical of the sort of process theology
lots of things that God can't do
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's turn follows Goff's answer and is marked by explicit dialogue continuity.
moves.proposition: Process theology is a nearby view retaining divine goodness and love while limiting action through restricted knowledge or power, so Goff must distinguish his proposal from it.
moves.inventoryRationale: Introduces a substantive neighboring-theory challenge rather than treating Goff's model as the only finite theism.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I'm very sympathetic with with their general approach
I'm open to God's knowledge being limited in that way
moves.attributionBasis: Goff directly answers Oppy's process-theology question.

responseComponents.component: Goff accepts kinship with process and open theism and allows that future contingents may not be knowable, while declining commitment to every process-theology detail.

moves.proposition: Goff is sympathetic but agnostic about process and open theism, and concedes that God's knowledge may be limited where no future fact yet exists.
moves.inventoryRationale: Records an important qualification and revision of his earlier claim that God is omniscient.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I don't think that's enough
God still could have made us without natural selection
moves.attributionBasis: Goff continues his direct answer to Oppy's process-theology comparison.

responseComponents.component: Mere ignorance of future contingents does not explain why God could not bypass natural selection; stronger creative limitations are still required.

moves.proposition: Process-style limitations on foreknowledge are insufficient to explain suffering because God might still have created intelligent beings without natural selection.
moves.inventoryRationale: Distinguishes Goff's specific power limit from a merely epistemically limited deity.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if you're perfectly good, you're going to care about our suffering
I find that hard to square
moves.attributionBasis: Goff clearly states his objection to Tim Mulgan's neighboring view.
moves.proposition: Anthropocentric purposivism is unstable if it says God is perfectly good yet indifferent to human suffering, since perfect goodness supplies reason to care even about lesser creatures.
moves.inventoryRationale: Assesses another nearby theistic alternative and explains why Goff retains divine goodness plus power limitation.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: committed to us having a reasonable amount of insight into divine psychology
there's still an issue there
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy directly responds to Goff's claim that a good designer predicts value.

responseComponents.component: The joint explanation assumes reliable insight into what a radically different divine being would value and do.
Fine-tuning likelihoods depend on the divine option set and psychology, neither of which is yet established.

moves.proposition: Goff's predictions require substantial insight into divine psychology, but a being radically unlike us may have unfamiliar values and creative options.
moves.inventoryRationale: Identifies a central under-support problem for both the purposive explanation and its claimed likelihood.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's significantly more expected
more likely than on chance
you don't have to say I totally understand divine psychology
moves.attributionBasis: Goff directly answers Oppy's divine-psychology objection.

responseComponents.component: Comparative support needs only the modest judgment that a value-caring creator makes life-permitting constants more expected than chance, not a complete divine psychology.

moves.proposition: Fine-tuning favors theism if a good creator makes life-permitting constants even significantly more expected than chance; complete knowledge of divine psychology is unnecessary.
moves.inventoryRationale: Gives Goff's calibrated answer to the likelihood objection.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the worries will be the same
another realm of creatures that we don't know about
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy substantively answers the moderator's metaethical proposal in his own turn.

responseComponents.component: Objective value alone does not show that humans are God's primary concern; unknown higher creatures could occupy that role.

moves.proposition: Appealing to objective moral facts does not eliminate the divine-psychology problem, because God might principally value unknown higher creatures and leave concern for humans to them.
moves.inventoryRationale: Preserves Oppy's answer that metaethics alone does not generate the needed prediction.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the answer to that question is yes
doesn't mean that God has more reason
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy clearly answers Goff's direct question about objective value.

responseComponents.component: Conceding that intelligent life has objective value does not by itself establish that God has proportionately greater reason to create it.

moves.proposition: Intelligent life may objectively have value without that fact alone giving God greater reason to care about or create it.
moves.inventoryRationale: Records a genuine concession on value alongside Oppy's denial of Goff's predictive inference.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: how many options are open to right creator
for all we know it turns out the numbers are about the same
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy directly responds to Goff's comparative expectation claim.

responseComponents.component: Without knowing the number and quality of worlds open to God or the divine choice procedure, this world's likelihood under theism may be no better than under chance.

moves.proposition: The probability of this world under a creator depends on the available alternatives and selection procedure; absent that information, theism's likelihood may equal chance.
moves.inventoryRationale: Sharpens the objection by separating value-fitting from a positive comparative likelihood.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there aren't possibilities beyond that that are open to God
delimiting the range of possibility
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy responds to Goff's proposal to build creative limits into the hypothesis.

responseComponents.component: Specifying God's powers also assumes a restricted space of possible worlds, so the proposed limit requires independent modal support.

moves.proposition: Goff's 'this or nothing' restriction is not merely a claim about divine power but a substantive delimitation of which worlds are possible.
moves.inventoryRationale: Exposes the modal burden embedded in the suffering solution.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the beginning state is necessary
they couldn't have been otherwise
It's not arbitrary in an important sense
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's uninterrupted response to the discussion of 'this or nothing.'

responseComponents.component: If all possible worlds share the initial state, the constants are necessary rather than chance-selected.
A necessity-based modal explanation need not treat fine-tuning like a contingent purposive inscription.

moves.proposition: On an Aristotelian modal theory where worlds share an initial history, constants fixed in the initial state are necessary and thereby non-arbitrary.
moves.inventoryRationale: Presents Oppy's principal naturalistic modal account of fine-tuning.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: If you think there's the same range of possibilities
fine tuning isn't evidence for anything
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy continues the same modal argument.

responseComponents.component: If constants arise through an indeterministic transition with equal ranges under both theories, the evidence does not discriminate.
Equal possibility ranges block the claim that life-permitting values are more expected under a creator.

moves.proposition: If constants become fixed indeterministically and theism and naturalism permit the same range, both explain the result equally and fine-tuning favors neither.
moves.inventoryRationale: Supplies Oppy's alternative branch if the constants are not initially necessary.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we're working with epistemic probability
epistemic probability not metaphysical probability
not a sufficient response to the finetuning argument
moves.attributionBasis: Goff directly answers Oppy's modal account.

responseComponents.component: Metaphysical necessity does not erase epistemic evidential comparison, just as a necessary identity can still be learned from evidence.
Bayesian assessment uses epistemic rather than metaphysical alternatives, so restricting metaphysical possibility does not by itself produce a draw.

moves.proposition: Fine-tuning concerns epistemic probability, so even metaphysically necessary constants can provide evidence when agents rationally consider epistemic alternatives.
moves.inventoryRationale: States the methodological divide underlying Goff's reply to Oppy's modality.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we don't actually have that awesome evidence
they have a very different standing
They seem different to me
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy directly answers Goff's awesome-evidence analogy.

responseComponents.component: The Quran case is a counterfactual with an impossible antecedent on Oppy's view, whereas fine-tuning is actual evidence.
Temporarily granting that an impossible counterfactual would be evidential does not commit Oppy's actual theory to treating existing fine-tuning identically.

moves.proposition: The awesome-evidence analogy fails because the imagined Quran inscription is unavailable and impossible on Oppy's theory, while fine-tuning is actual evidence with different standing.
moves.inventoryRationale: Gives Oppy's principal direct rebuttal to Goff's analogy.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I'm not a basian
compare the total theories
fit with the evidence on the one hand and simplicity on the other
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's explicit methodological response.

responseComponents.component: Oppy rejects the Bayesian framework and instead compares complete theories by simplicity and fit with actual evidence.

moves.proposition: Worldviews should be compared as total theories by simplicity and fit with actual evidence, not by Bayesian conditionalization over epistemic possibilities.
moves.inventoryRationale: States Oppy's alternative theory-comparison method and explains why Goff's probability reply does not engage it.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the domain in which it's actually appropriate to talk about probability
it doesn't extend to things like philosophy
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy clearly answers the moderator's request for his anti-Bayesian rationale.
moves.proposition: Bayesian probability is appropriate in scientific domains but does not straightforwardly extend to philosophical worldview comparison.
moves.inventoryRationale: Provides Oppy's concise domain-based reason for rejecting Goff's preferred method.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: phenomenal states just are brain states
phenomenal states play a role in the causation of behavior
easily accommodated by the identity theory
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's uninterrupted answer on psychophysical harmony.

responseComponents.component: Identity theory denies a gap between phenomenal and relevant brain states and allows consciousness to cause behavior.
The intuition that pain causes behavior is naturally accommodated without adding a purposive supernatural explanation.

moves.proposition: On identity theory, phenomenal states are brain states and causally contribute to behavior, so Oppy sees no independent psychophysical-harmony problem.
moves.inventoryRationale: States Oppy's basic naturalistic response to Goff's consciousness challenge.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: when they're working out the prior for naturalism
Now that's not fair
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy directly explains his criticism of the cited Bayesian paper.
moves.proposition: The psychophysical-harmony paper treats background knowledge asymmetrically, invoking it for theism's prior while ignoring it for naturalism's prior.
moves.inventoryRationale: Preserves Oppy's specific methodological criticism rather than a generic rejection of Bayesianism.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: creatures that were wired up that way wouldn't procreate
the story didn't hang together
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy answers the moderator's summary of the disharmony scenario.

responseComponents.component: A creature whose behavior systematically avoided pleasure would fail to reproduce, so the proposed disharmonious alternative is not evolutionarily stable.

moves.proposition: Systematically disharmonious creatures that behaviorally avoid pleasure would rapidly become extinct, so the proposed alternative does not form a coherent evolutionary scenario.
moves.inventoryRationale: Adds natural selection as a direct constraint on alleged psychophysical alternatives.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Couldn't something different a non-concious mechanism have done exactly the same stuff
why consciousness rather than non-concious mechanisms
moves.attributionBasis: Goff explicitly separates and states his second question to Oppy.

responseComponents.component: Identity and mental causation show that consciousness does causal work but do not explain why evolution used consciousness rather than a nonconscious functional duplicate.
Evolutionary instability of one disharmonious design does not exclude all nonconscious mechanisms capable of the same adaptive behavior.

moves.proposition: Even if consciousness is identical with causal brain states and aids survival, Oppy has not explained why an equally functional nonconscious mechanism was not selected.
moves.inventoryRationale: Precisely preserves Goff's explanatory rather than anti-physicalist objection.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: particular evolutionary pressures that our ancestors were under
it is contingent
set of course
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy answers Goff's request for an explanation of the evolutionary route.

responseComponents.component: Contingent early adaptations and path-dependent evolutionary pressures can explain why one workable mechanism arose rather than another.

moves.proposition: Evolution often selects one among many workable solutions through contingent pressures and path dependence, after which later development is constrained by the established trajectory.
moves.inventoryRationale: Supplies Oppy's positive contingent-naturalistic answer to the demand for contrastive explanation.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: consciousness is in the animal kingdom
what's distinctive about human beings
not necessarily tied to consciousness
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy has the final substantive turn in the consciousness exchange.

responseComponents.component: Consciousness may be widespread in relatively simple animals, whereas distinctly human conceptual and reasoning capacities may arise from later communication adaptations.
Separating ancient consciousness from later human reasoning weakens the claim that one unified purposive explanation is required.

moves.proposition: Consciousness may extend deep into the animal kingdom, while distinctively human reasoning arose later through communication and social pressures and is not necessarily constitutively tied to consciousness.
moves.inventoryRationale: Offers Oppy's more differentiated evolutionary account and marks its speculative status.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it all comes down to simplicity
theory to fit the data
lots of different gods
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's substantive answer to the audience question about finite polytheism.
moves.proposition: Finite polytheism remains possible, but multiplying gods and mixed psychologies increases complexity; one precisely limited good God better balances simplicity with fit to suffering.
moves.inventoryRationale: Directly covers the required finite-polytheism comparison without excluding it deductively.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a kind of de facto privacy
there's a difference between being in a state and observing the state
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's substantive answer to the audience question on mental privacy.
moves.proposition: Identity theory permits de facto mental privacy and a principled difference between occupying a phenomenal state and merely observing its physical realization.
moves.inventoryRationale: Covers the required mental-privacy issue and shows how Oppy reconciles it with physical identity.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: three aspects
the fewer primitive undefined terms you've got, the better
not much more to naturalism than scientific theory
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's substantive answer to the audience question on intrinsic probability.
moves.proposition: Theory simplicity depends on concise axiomatization, few primitives, and limited ontological commitments; because naturalism adds little beyond shared scientific theory, it is simplest overall.
moves.inventoryRationale: Provides Oppy's positive motion-level case for naturalism rather than merely criticizing theism.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: judge intrinsic probability roughly on simplicity
both my limited guard and naturalism are both pretty simple
moves.attributionBasis: Goff directly follows Oppy's answer on intrinsic probability.

responseComponents.component: Goff accepts simplicity as the main guide to intrinsic probability but denies that it clearly separates naturalism from his limited-God hypothesis.

moves.proposition: Intrinsic probability tracks simplicity, but both naturalism and Goff's precisely limited deity are comparatively simple theories.
moves.inventoryRationale: Records agreement on the criterion while preserving disagreement about its comparative result.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: God is a mind but a very different kind of mind
fundamental moral facts are part of God
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's substantive answer to the audience question concerning divine mentality.
moves.proposition: God is a radically different kind of mind: fundamental moral facts constitute divine motivation rather than ordinary beliefs and desires.
moves.inventoryRationale: Clarifies Goff's purposive-agent model and qualifies ordinary psychological descriptions of God.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
quoteEligibleExactSpans: justifying that kind of Aristotilian conception of modality
lots turns on that
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's direct substantive answer to the final moderator question.
moves.proposition: The strongest challenge to Oppy's current naturalism is justifying the Aristotelian conception of modality on which much of his account depends.
moves.inventoryRationale: Records Oppy's own principal vulnerability and its importance to his fine-tuning response.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
quoteEligibleExactSpans: my biggest source of doubt with fine-tuning is the evidence could change
you might be getting something wrong
moves.attributionBasis: Goff's direct substantive answer to the final moderator question.
moves.proposition: Goff's strongest doubts are that future physics may remove the fine-tuning datum and that difficult probability judgments may be mistaken.
moves.inventoryRationale: Records Goff's own account of the strongest evidential and technical challenges to finite theism.

selectionRationale: The inventory selects 40 chronologically ordered, independently assessable moves across six weighted clusters. It includes the debate's principal constructive cases, direct replies, qualifications, and concessions while excluding moderator content except where needed to identify a debater's substantive answer. The selected spans keep evidence-fitting distinct from positive comparative support, simplicity distinct from likelihood, criticism of naturalism distinct from support for finite theism, and finite theism distinct from classical omnipotent theism. Each section contains moves from both sides, no side has more than four moves in a section, and every move contacts a side-specific burden bridge.
